payload.name: waveform-coding
payload.scope: So a continuous signal can be carried and stored at a fixed reduced bit rate with its waveform shape preserved, in contrast to parametric coding, which transmits only a model of the source.

definition.body: Waveform-coding is a human-made family of signal-coding procedures that encode the signal's own waveform - the sequence of sample amplitudes - rather than a model of the source, so a continuous signal can be carried or stored at a fixed reduced bit rate with the waveform shape preserved. The family's procedures act on the waveform itself: pulse-code modulation quantizes the sample values directly; delta modulation encodes the difference between successive samples; adaptive differential pulse-code modulation quantizes the prediction error against an adaptive predictor; sigma-delta modulation emits an oversampled one-bit feedback stream. Parameters that define the class: (1) the bit commitment to the waveform, fixed or adaptive; (2) the representation of each sample - direct amplitude level, successive difference, or prediction error; (3) the reconstruction rule that maps the code word back to a sample. Persistence mechanism: specified in the ITU-T G.711, G.721, G.726 standards and the CD Red Book, described in the speech-coding literature as the waveform-coding class alongside parametric and hybrid coding, and implemented in telephony, music disc, and audio-coding practice. e.g.: the G.711 mu-law PCM codec in a T1 voice path; the G.726 24 kbit/s ADPCM codec in an ISDN voice channel; the 16-bit linear PCM of a Red Book CD track | not: linear predictive coding which transmits a model of the vocal tract rather than the waveform; the code-excited linear prediction of G.729 which synthesizes speech from codebook excitation through a synthesis filter; transform coding of a coefficient vector in the frequency domain [formal: codificatio formae undae | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: So that a continuous signal can be carried at one bit per sample, below the rate where a multi-bit quantizer is worth its complexity, with a one-sample prediction stage preserving most of the waveform.

definition.body: Delta modulation is a human-made one-bit predictive waveform-coding procedure that transmits, for each new sample, only the sign of the difference between the sample and the previously reconstructed value, so a continuous signal can be carried on one bit per sample. Procedure: (1) a predictor holds the last reconstructed sample; (2) the encoder compares the new sample with it and transmits one bit, up or down; (3) the decoder reconstructs the sample as the previous sample plus or minus a step, fixed in basic delta modulation and adapted to the signal slope in adaptive delta modulation. Parameters: (1) the bit commitment, one bit per sample; (2) the step size, fixed or adaptive; (3) the predictor order, the previous sample in first-order delta modulation, a linear combination in differential forms; (4) the sampling rate, at the Nyquist rate in classic delta modulation, where oversampled one-bit variants with noise-shaped feedback are sigma-delta modulation instead. Persistence mechanism: proposed by Zeller in 1948 for long-distance telephone lines, realized in Bell System first-order delta-modulation voice experiments at 256 kbit/s, carried in the differential lineage of the ITU-T G.721 and G.726 standards, and described in the coding literature as the one-bit ancestor of differential pulse-code modulation. e.g.: Zeller's 1948 delta modulation proposal for long-distance telephone lines; first-order delta modulation voice channel at 256 kbit/s in Bell System experiments; one-bit delta modulation telemetry channel in a satellite downlink | not: sigma-delta modulation (oversampled one-bit noise-shaped feedback stream); pulse-code modulation (multi-bit quantizer on the full sample, no prediction stage); adaptive differential pulse-code modulation (multi-bit prediction-error quantizer, G.726) [formal: modulatio deltae | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

definition.body: A log-law quantizer is a human-made quantization structure whose step sizes scale logarithmically with signal amplitude, so that small amplitudes receive fine steps and large amplitudes receive coarse steps, achieving a near-constant signal-to-quantization-noise ratio across the input dynamic range. Procedure: the quantizer maps input amplitudes to quantization levels using a piecewise-logarithmic step-size function — at each amplitude level a, the step size Δ(a) = Δ₀ · r^(⌊a⌋) for base rate Δ₀ and growth ratio r > 1, producing a nonuniform partition of the amplitude range that preserves perceptual fidelity. Parameters: (1) the step-size growth ratio r, typically 1.5–2.0 per step; (2) the number of quantization levels, commonly 64 in predictive codecs; (3) the dynamic range covered, the ratio between maximum and minimum step sizes. definition.body: A mu-law nonlinearity is a human-made piecewise-logarithmic companding compressor curve that fits a wide dynamic range signal into a small number of uniform quantization steps. Procedure: (1) compress the input amplitude through the mu-law curve mu(x) = sign(x)·ln(1+mu·|x|)/ln(1+mu), (2) apply a uniform 8-bit quantizer to the compressed value, (3) at the receiver expand through the inverse curve to reconstruct a linear output. payload.name: cepstral-mean-subtraction
payload.scope: So that cepstral feature vectors are centered and normalized for robust spectral shape comparison across sessions.

definition.body: Cepstral-mean-subtraction is a human-made normalization procedure that centers cepstral coefficient vectors by subtracting their frame-wise or session-wise mean, removing static offset to emphasize spectral shape over absolute level. Procedure: (1) compute the mean of each cepstral coefficient dimension over a sliding window (typically 301-501 ms) or an entire utterance/session, (2) subtract that mean from each cepstral coefficient value, (3) output the zero-mean cepstral coefficients. Parameters: (1) the window length for mean computation, (2) the cepstral coefficient dimensions included, (3) whether to apply per-frame or global mean. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech recognition frontends such as Kaldi's cmvn and apply-cmvn tools, HTK's cepstral mean normalization, and standard feature normalization pipelines in speaker recognition systems. e.g.: Kaldi's cmvn tool applied to MFCC features in the LibriSpeech speech recognition pipeline; HTK cepstral mean normalization applied to Aurora-4 evaluation features; the apply-cmvn step in a Kaldi i-vector speaker recognition frontend | not: cepstral-mean (the scalar value itself, not the normalization procedure); cepstral-variance-normalization (divides by standard deviation in addition to subtracting mean, not just mean removal) [formal: subtractio medi cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-peak-to-average-ratio
payload.scope: So that the prominence of periodic structure in the cepstrum can be measured as a single scalar for pitch and voicing detection.

definition.body: Cepstral-peak-to-average-ratio is a human-made scalar feature computed from cepstral coefficients that measures the prominence of the dominant periodic component relative to the overall cepstral energy. Procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of a signal frame, (2) identify the maximum-magnitude cepstral coefficient within a quefrency range of interest (typically corresponding to the expected pitch period), (3) compute the arithmetic mean of all cepstral coefficients in that range, (4) divide the peak value by the mean to obtain the ratio. Parameters: (1) the quefrency range for peak detection, (2) whether to use absolute magnitude or signed value, (3) the number of cepstral coefficients included. Persistence mechanism: used in pitch detection and voicing decision systems, described in speech processing literature for periodicity measurement, and implemented in research speech analysis toolkits. e.g.: peak-to-average cepstral ratio in a pitch detection algorithm for the Aurora-4 speech recognition evaluation; cepstral peak prominence measurement in Kaldi's pitch estimation tools; the cepstral peak-to-mean ratio in the CMU Sphinx voicing decision pipeline | not: cepstrum-energy (sum of squared coefficients, not peak-to-average ratio); cepstral-peak-picking (identifies peak locations, not the ratio of peak to mean) [formal: ratio acmen-medii cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]
